items.termEn: Dark roast coffee always contains more caffeine than light roast coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Roasting changes the flavor and color of the bean, but most of the caffeine stays intact.
That is why a dark roast and a light roast from the same beans carry similar caffeine levels.
Light roast can match dark roast in caffeine.

items.termEn: Arabica contains on average more caffeine than robusta.
items.explanationShort:
Robusta has roughly twice the caffeine of arabica.
That difference comes from the plant species itself, not from how it is roasted or brewed.
Robusta, not arabica, is the higher-caffeine bean.

items.termEn: Decaffeinated coffee contains absolutely zero caffeine.
items.explanationShort:
Decaf removes most caffeine, but never all of it.
Because of that, a typical decaf still contains 5 to 15 mg of caffeine per cup.
Decaf still has a kick, just smaller.

items.termEn: An espresso has more caffeine than a regular cup of drip coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Espresso is highly concentrated but tiny, about 1 oz (30 ml) per shot.
Drip coffee is milder per sip but much larger, around 8 to 12 oz.
Stronger taste does not mean more caffeine.

items.termEn: Caffeine in a cup depends mostly on how long the coffee is brewed.
items.explanationShort:
Brew time plays a role, but species, dose, and cup size matter more.
That is why an espresso and a French press can carry similar caffeine.
Bean type and cup size beat brew time.

items.termEn: Caffeine sensitivity is the same for everyone.
items.explanationShort:
Caffeine affects people differently because genetics, habits, age, medications, and other factors can change sensitivity and metabolism.
The same dose can feel very different from one person to another.
There is no single personal limit for everyone.

items.termEn: A coffee at 3 PM is always out of your system by midnight.
items.explanationShort:
In most adults, half the caffeine is still in the body 5 hours after drinking.
After about 10 hours, most of it is finally gone.
Late coffee can still echo at midnight.

items.termEn: Robusta coffee is always lower quality than arabica.
items.explanationShort:
Arabica and robusta are different coffee species, not quality grades.
Robusta generally contains more caffeine and has a different sensory profile, but either species can be produced well or poorly.
Species alone does not guarantee quality.

items.termEn: A light roast has a weaker flavor than a dark roast.
items.explanationShort:
Light roasts taste fruity and bright.
Dark roasts taste smoky and bitter.
The roast changes taste, not strength.

items.termEn: For most healthy adults, the daily caffeine safety limit is 200 mg.
items.explanationShort:
For most healthy adults, the EFSA considers daily caffeine intake up to 400 mg unlikely to raise safety concerns.
That is a population-level safety reference, not a target or a guarantee of comfort.
200 mg is the single-dose reference, not the daily one.

items.termEn: Cold brew and iced coffee use different brewing methods.
items.explanationShort:
Cold brew steeps grounds in cold water for 12 to 24 hours.
Iced coffee is hot-brewed coffee poured over ice.
Same beans, two different drinks.

items.termEn: Pouring hot-brewed coffee over ice makes it taste as strong as regular hot coffee.
items.explanationShort:
When hot coffee hits ice, the ice melts immediately and dilutes the drink.
The same coffee poured over ice always tastes weaker than the same coffee served hot.
Hot cup, stronger. Iced cup, weaker.

items.termEn: A cappuccino usually contains more milk than a latte.
items.explanationShort:
A cappuccino uses less milk and more foam than a latte.
A latte is built with much more steamed milk, which makes it larger and softer in taste.
The latte is milk-heavier, not the cappuccino.

items.termEn: A flat white usually contains less milk and less foam than a latte.
items.explanationShort:
A flat white is served in a smaller cup, typically around 5 oz, with thinner, velvety foam.
A latte is usually larger, around 8 to 12 oz, with more milk and a softer taste.
Flat white, bold. Latte, creamy.

items.termEn: A cortado is commonly close to equal parts espresso and warm milk.
items.explanationShort:
A traditional cortado uses a small amount of warm milk to soften espresso without turning it into a milk-heavy drink.
Recipes vary by café, but the drink is commonly close to a 1:1 balance.
Small drink, espresso-forward.

items.termEn: Grind size has a major effect on how an espresso tastes.
items.explanationShort:
Grind size changes how quickly water can extract soluble material from coffee.
On espresso, small grind adjustments can noticeably change flow rate and taste.
Grind is one of the main dialing-in variables.

items.termEn: In France, a café usually means a large filter coffee.
items.explanationShort:
When you sit down at a French cafe, the default order is a tiny espresso.
It is served in a small cup, not a large mug.
In France, un cafe is usually a shot, not a big filter coffee.

items.termEn: A café gourmand in France is a coffee served with several small desserts.
items.explanationShort:
A café gourmand pairs one coffee with a selection of small desserts on the side.
It is often ordered at the end of a meal as a lighter alternative to a full dessert.
Coffee plus sweets on one plate, not just a cup.

items.termEn: A single espresso is typically 60–90 ml (about 2–3 oz).
items.explanationShort:
An espresso is roughly the size of a shot glass, about 25 to 35 ml.
Most people expect more liquid, but that small size is what makes it so concentrated.
A standard espresso is much smaller than 2 to 3 oz.

items.termEn: A good starting ratio for brewed coffee is 55 g per liter, or 2 oz per 32 oz.
items.explanationShort:
Around 55 g of coffee per liter of water is a widely used reference point for brewed coffee.
From there, the ratio can be adjusted to taste and to the brewing method.
It is a starting point, not a fixed law.

items.termEn: Most coffee brews best with fully boiling water at 212°F (100°C).
items.explanationShort:
A common reference range for brewed coffee is about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
A full rolling boil is hotter than that target, and temperature mainly changes extraction rate.
Just off the boil is a useful starting point.

items.termEn: A blade grinder produces a more consistent grind than a burr grinder.
items.explanationShort:
Blade grinders chop randomly, producing a mix of fine dust and large chunks in the same batch.
Burr grinders crush at a fixed distance, so every particle comes out a similar size.
The burr grinder is the consistency tool, not the blade grinder.

items.termEn: Coffee that tastes sour and bitter at the same time may have an uneven grind.
items.explanationShort:
Uneven grind means some bits over-brew (bitter) and others under-brew (sour).
A consistent grind lets every particle brew at the same rate.
Sour plus bitter together usually means the grinder.

items.termEn: Tap water is the best way to limit limescale buildup in a coffee machine.
items.explanationShort:
Limescale comes from minerals such as calcium and magnesium in water.
Water treatment that actually reduces hardness can slow scale buildup; not every household filter removes those minerals.
Lower hardness, less scale.

items.termEn: A weak cup can come from using too little coffee.
items.explanationShort:
The amount of coffee directly affects strength.
Too little coffee can make the drink taste thin, even if the brew method is fine.
Too little coffee, weaker cup.

items.termEn: Many hot-coffee recipes use water below a full rolling boil.
items.explanationShort:
A common brewing reference range is roughly 195–205°F (90–96°C).
That is below 212°F (100°C) at sea level.
Boiling is not required for good extraction.

items.termEn: Changing brew-water temperature changes how quickly coffee extracts.
items.explanationShort:
Hotter water generally speeds extraction, while cooler water slows it.
Taste depends on the final strength and extraction as well as temperature, grind, time, and dose.
Temperature matters, but it is not a one-variable taste switch.

items.termEn: Leaving coffee to brew longer than recommended makes it stronger and more enjoyable.
items.explanationShort:
Longer contact time can increase extraction, but more extraction is not automatically more enjoyable.
The useful brew time depends on the method, grind, dose, and desired result.
Longer is not automatically better.

items.termEn: If coffee tastes weak, the grind is often too coarse.
items.explanationShort:
A coarser grind lets water pass too quickly, pulling less flavor.
Going finer slows the water and extracts more from the grounds.
Weak cup, try a finer grind.

items.termEn: Ground coffee stays fresh longer after opening than whole beans do.
items.explanationShort:
Every time you open the bag, coffee is exposed to oxygen.
Ground coffee has far more surface area exposed, so it stales faster than whole beans.
Whole beans hold flavor longer once the bag is open.

items.termEn: Ground coffee can keep its flavor as long as whole beans after opening the bag.
items.explanationShort:
Grinding multiplies the surface area exposed to air.
That is why aromas escape much faster from ground coffee than from whole beans.
Grind fresh, not in advance.

items.termEn: A large bag of coffee keeps its full flavor for weeks after opening.
items.explanationShort:
Once a coffee bag is opened, oxygen and repeated exposure gradually reduce aroma and flavor.
How fast that happens depends on roast, packaging, storage, and how often the bag is opened.
Large bags are harder to finish at peak freshness.

items.termEn: A grinder that has not been cleaned in weeks can make fresh coffee taste stale.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee oils build up inside the grinder with each use.
Over time, those oils turn rancid and contaminate the next batch of grounds.
Clean grinder, fresh taste every time.

items.termEn: Preheating a coffee cup lowers aroma and temperature from the first sip.
items.explanationShort:
A cold cup pulls heat from the coffee the moment it is poured.
That temperature drop mutes the aromas before you even take the first sip.
Preheating helps because the cup stops stealing heat from the coffee.

items.termEn: Coffee aroma starts changing as soon as brewing ends.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee releases volatile aromatic compounds continuously after brewing.
As the cup sits and cools, its aroma profile changes and some volatile aromas dissipate.
Freshly brewed coffee does not stay aromatically identical.

items.termEn: Stirring a freshly brewed cup can make its flavor more consistent from sip to sip.
items.explanationShort:
Freshly brewed coffee can have temperature and concentration differences within the cup.
A gentle stir mixes the beverage before tasting.
Stirring is a simple way to make the cup more uniform.

items.termEn: Letting coffee cool for a few minutes can bring out more sweetness and acidity.
items.explanationShort:
Temperature affects how taste receptors pick up different flavors.
As coffee cools, acidity and sweetness become more noticeable while bitterness softens.
Hot coffee, bitter edge. Cooler coffee, more sweetness.

items.termEn: A one-way valve on a coffee bag keeps gas inside and lets air in.
items.explanationShort:
Freshly roasted beans release CO2 for days and need a way to let it out.
The one-way valve lets that gas escape without allowing oxygen back in.
It vents gas out while blocking air from coming in.

items.termEn: Even well-sealed pre-ground coffee goes stale faster than whole beans.
items.explanationShort:
Grinding exposes every tiny particle to air, so aromas start escaping within minutes.
Whole beans, with far less surface area, hold their flavor much longer.
Grind fresh, taste fresh.

items.termEn: Coffee tastes best the instant it comes out of the roaster.
items.explanationShort:
Freshly roasted beans release carbon dioxide for days.
A short resting period can make brewing more even, especially for espresso.
Fresh does not always mean same-day fresh.

items.termEn: A coffee machine can taste cleaner after washing even if it still needs descaling.
items.explanationShort:
Washing removes coffee oils and residue that affect taste, but it does not remove mineral scale inside the machine.
That is why a machine can taste cleaner and still suffer from limescale problems.
Clean taste does not mean scale is gone.

items.termEn: On a home espresso machine, grind changes are a minor detail for taste.
items.explanationShort:
The grind controls how much flavor the water picks up.
The right grind can make a shot richer, sharper, or more balanced.
On espresso, grind changes the cup immediately.

items.termEn: Pressing harder on espresso grounds does not fix a weak or bitter shot.
items.explanationShort:
A weak or bitter espresso usually traces back to the grind or the dose, not the pressure.
Pressing harder on the grounds does not change either of those variables.
More pressure is not the answer.

items.termEn: Cold brew usually tastes more bitter than hot-brewed coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Cold brew is often perceived as smoother or less bitter than hot-brewed coffee, although the result depends on coffee, roast, ratio, and recipe.
Different extraction conditions create a different sensory balance.
Cold brew is not inherently the more bitter method.

items.termEn: For the same brew setup, a finer grind generally increases extraction compared with a coarser grind.
items.explanationShort:
Finer particles expose more surface area and usually slow water flow in percolation brewing.
That tends to increase extraction when other variables stay similar.
Grind changes extraction, not just texture.

items.termEn: Espresso crema can taste bitter even when the shot underneath is balanced.
items.explanationShort:
Crema is made of concentrated oils and gases released during extraction.
That layer often tastes harsher and more bitter than the liquid espresso below it.
Beautiful crema, not always the best sip alone.

items.termEn: Coffee left on a hot plate stays fresh for up to an hour.
items.explanationShort:
Heat does not stop working on coffee once brewing ends.
After 20 to 30 minutes on a hot plate, flavors go flat and bitterness increases.
Thermos or nothing, not a hot plate.

items.termEn: A machine rinsed with water after each use still builds up oils that turn rancid over time.
items.explanationShort:
Water clears visible residue but cannot dissolve the oils that cling to the machine's interior.
Those oils turn rancid over time and taint every cup that follows.
Rinse clears water, not oil.

items.termEn: For most healthy adults, the safe single-dose caffeine limit is about 100 mg.
items.explanationShort:
200 mg per dose is the safety threshold for most healthy adults, roughly one double espresso.
That is a safety guideline, not a comfort guarantee.
100 mg is not the usual upper safe single-dose reference for healthy adults.

items.termEn: Coffee-to-water ratio is one of the main controls on beverage strength.
items.explanationShort:
Using more coffee relative to water generally produces a stronger beverage, all else equal.
The brewing method still matters for extraction and flavor.
Ratio is a major strength control, not the only variable.

items.termEn: Coffee can taste worse if old coffee grounds are left inside the filter.
items.explanationShort:
Old grounds leave stale, rancid oils behind in the filter after each brew.
When new water passes through, those oils dissolve directly into the next cup.
Yesterday's grounds are ruining today's cup.

items.termEn: A cappuccino usually has more foam than a latte.
items.explanationShort:
A cappuccino typically uses less milk and a thicker layer of foam than a latte.
A latte usually has more steamed milk and only a thin layer of foam.
Exact recipes vary by café.

items.termEn: A thin, watery espresso is often a sign the grind is too coarse.
items.explanationShort:
Water needs enough time in contact with the grounds to pull out the full flavor.
When the shot runs too fast, most of the flavor compounds stay behind in the puck.
Rushed water skips the flavor.

items.termEn: A metal filter makes coffee taste cleaner and lighter than a paper filter.
items.explanationShort:
Paper filters absorb oils that pass freely through a metal filter.
Without those oils, paper-filtered coffee tastes cleaner and lighter.
Paper catches what metal lets through.

items.termEn: Coffee stored in the freezer can pick up odors if it is not truly airtight.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee easily absorbs odors and moisture from its surroundings.
That is why freezer storage only works when the container is truly airtight.
No airtight seal, no flavor protection.

items.termEn: Freezing coffee can help preserve it for long-term storage if it is truly airtight.
items.explanationShort:
Freezing can slow staling, but only if the coffee is sealed away from moisture and odors.
With a truly airtight container, the freezer can help preserve flavor longer.
Freeze only if the seal is airtight.

items.termEn: Grinding coffee right before brewing usually gives a fresher-tasting cup than grinding it the night before.
items.explanationShort:
Grinding exposes much more coffee surface area to oxygen.
That accelerates aroma loss, so grinding immediately before brewing usually preserves more fresh aroma than grinding the night before.
Grind closer to brew time for fresher flavor.

items.termEn: Leaving French-press coffee in contact with the grounds well past the target steep time can increase bitterness.
items.explanationShort:
French-press recipes commonly use a few minutes of immersion before the coffee is separated from the grounds.
Keeping the beverage in contact with the grounds changes extraction over time.
Decanting after the target steep helps stop that contact.

items.termEn: The fridge helps coffee beans stay fresh by keeping them cool and dry.
items.explanationShort:
The fridge is full of moisture and strong odors that coffee readily absorbs.
That absorption damages the flavor instead of protecting it.
The fridge steals flavor instead of saving it.

items.termEn: The flat white first became popular in Australia and New Zealand.
items.explanationShort:
The flat white emerged in Australia and New Zealand in the 1980s.
Both countries are closely tied to its rise and still debate the exact origin.
Australasia made it famous.

items.termEn: Adding water to a bitter espresso removes the bitterness at the source.
items.explanationShort:
Adding water dilutes the drink, but it does not touch the source of the bitterness.
Bitterness usually comes from grind size or brew time, and water changes neither.
Dilution is not a real fix.

items.termEn: A macchiato is usually a milk-heavy drink like a latte.
items.explanationShort:
A macchiato is built on espresso as its base, with only a small mark of milk added.
That small amount of milk softens the edge slightly without changing the drink's character.
Mostly espresso, barely any milk.

items.termEn: A French press and pour-over coffee produce the same mouthfeel.
items.explanationShort:
A French press lets oils and fine particles pass freely into the cup, creating a heavier texture.
Pour-over coffee usually uses a paper filter, which produces a cleaner and lighter result.
Same beans, different mouthfeel entirely.

items.termEn: A capsule machine and a traditional espresso machine always produce the same cup.
items.explanationShort:
Capsule systems and traditional espresso machines use different doses, grind control, pressure profiles, and user inputs.
They can both make concentrated coffee, but they are not guaranteed to produce the same result.
Same category does not mean identical cup.

items.termEn: Regular oat milk froths as easily as cow's milk under a steam wand.
items.explanationShort:
Cow's milk naturally has the proteins that help foam hold together.
Oat milk usually needs a barista formula, more time, or better technique to foam well.
Oat can work beautifully, but not always as easily.

items.termEn: Soy milk stays perfectly smooth in hot coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Soy milk is sensitive to heat and acidity, and espresso delivers both at once.
When the two meet, the acidity destabilizes the soy protein and causes it to split.
Hot acidic espresso and soy do not always mix.

items.termEn: All plant-based milks leave coffee tasting basically the same.
items.explanationShort:
Each plant milk has its own flavor profile that it adds to the drink.
Coconut brings tropical notes, almond adds nuttiness, and oat contributes mild sweetness.
Plant milk choice changes what the coffee tastes like.

items.termEn: Ordering a doppio gives you about the same caffeine as a single espresso.
items.explanationShort:
A doppio is two espresso shots pulled together.
Since each shot contains roughly 60 to 75 mg of caffeine, a doppio roughly doubles that.
A doppio has much more caffeine than a single shot.

items.termEn: Specialty coffee helped make lighter roasts more popular again.
items.explanationShort:
Specialty coffee put more focus on origin, processing, and distinct flavor notes.
That helped bring lighter roasts back into favor, since they preserve more acidity and character than darker roasts.
Specialty coffee pushed lighter roasts back into the spotlight.

items.termEn: Oat milk was the main plant-based milk in US coffee shops before soy milk became popular.
items.explanationShort:
Soy milk appeared in US coffee shops well before oat milk's recent rise.
Oat milk became popular later, especially in espresso drinks.
Soy came first; oat came later.

items.termEn: Coconut milk froths just as reliably as oat milk under a steam wand.
items.explanationShort:
Coconut milk is high in fat but low in protein, and protein is what creates stable foam.
Oat milk has more body and produces a creamier microfoam under steam.
Same wand, different foam.

items.termEn: Robusta makes up more than half of the world's coffee exports.
items.explanationShort:
Arabica and robusta shares change from crop year to crop year.
Robusta is a major part of global coffee trade, but it does not consistently make up more than half of world coffee exports.
The mix changes; robusta is not the majority by default.

items.termEn: Coffee shop prices can be affected by changes in world coffee prices.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee shops buy beans whose prices move with world coffee markets.
When green coffee costs rise, that increase can pass through roasters and eventually to the counter.
Global price, local cup.

items.termEn: Kenya is known for producing robusta coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Kenya grows almost exclusively arabica at high altitude.
That combination produces a coffee prized for bright, fruity notes of berry and citrus.
Kenyan coffee is fruity and bright, not bold.

items.termEn: Coffee ground an hour before brewing tastes just as fresh as coffee ground right before.
items.explanationShort:
Aromatic compounds start escaping the moment coffee is ground.
That is why grinding right before brewing keeps more of those aromas in the cup.
Ground fresh, more aroma. Ground ahead, less.

items.termEn: An americano ends up with lower caffeine than its espresso base.
items.explanationShort:
An americano is made by adding hot water to an espresso shot to lengthen the drink.
The espresso base stays the same, so the caffeine stays the same regardless of cup size.
Water changes strength, not total caffeine.

items.termEn: Limescale in a coffee machine affects flavor but leaves the machine unharmed.
items.explanationShort:
Heavy limescale restricts water flow and makes the machine work harder.
Over time, that can damage performance as well as affect taste.
Scale hurts the machine, not just the cup.

items.termEn: A hardness-reducing water filter can help reduce limescale buildup in a coffee machine.
items.explanationShort:
Limescale forms from dissolved hardness minerals.
A treatment that reduces those minerals can slow scale buildup.
The important part is hardness reduction, not simply passing water through any filter.

items.termEn: Two coffees from the same farm can taste completely different depending on their processing.
items.explanationShort:
Natural processing dries the bean with its fruit still on, adding sweetness and body to the final cup.
Washed processing removes the fruit first, producing a cleaner, brighter flavor.
Same farm, different cup.

items.termEn: Most of the world's coffee is consumed where it is grown.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee is heavily traded internationally from tropical producing countries to consumer markets around the world.
Large producing countries also drink coffee domestically, but global consumption is not confined mainly to where coffee is grown.
Coffee is a global trade crop.

items.termEn: An espresso blend can include robusta; 100% arabica is not required.
items.explanationShort:
Espresso blends may use arabica, robusta, or both.
Robusta can contribute body, bitterness, caffeine, and crema, while arabica contributes a different sensory profile.
The blend choice is a recipe decision, not a purity rule.

items.termEn: The United States grows most of the coffee it drinks.
items.explanationShort:
The United States imports the overwhelming majority of the coffee it consumes.
There is domestic production in Hawaii and limited production elsewhere, but it is tiny compared with US consumption.
Most coffee in American cups is imported.

items.termEn: Italy grows most of the coffee it drinks.
items.explanationShort:
Italy is world-famous for its espresso culture and roasting expertise.
But coffee only grows in tropical climates near the equator, far from Italy's geography.
Italian coffee culture runs on imported beans.

items.termEn: China produces most of the coffee it drinks.
items.explanationShort:
China does produce coffee, mainly in the Yunnan province.
But domestic production falls far short of the country's growing consumption, so most comes from imports.
China drinks far more coffee than it grows.

items.termEn: Brazil exports far more coffee than it consumes domestically.
items.explanationShort:
Brazil is both the world's largest coffee producer and a significant consumer at home.
Even so, it exports far more than it keeps, supplying coffee markets around the world.
Exports dominate, domestic use is smaller.

items.termEn: Most Colombian coffee bags found in US stores contain arabica.
items.explanationShort:
Colombia's high altitude and climate are ideal conditions for arabica cultivation.
That is why the country grows arabica almost exclusively.
Colombian bag usually means arabica.

items.termEn: Finland has historically ranked among the world's highest coffee-consuming countries per person.
items.explanationShort:
Nordic countries have long appeared near the top of per-capita coffee consumption statistics.
Finland is frequently among the leaders.
Per-capita rankings can vary by dataset and year.

items.termEn: Robusta is widely used in instant coffee, and Vietnam is a major robusta producer.
items.explanationShort:
Vietnam is one of the world's largest producers of robusta.
Robusta is widely used in instant coffee because of its availability, caffeine content, and flavor profile.
Instant coffee is not limited to robusta, but the species is important to the category.

items.termEn: Wild Coffea arabica is native to Ethiopia and also occurs naturally in South Sudan.
items.explanationShort:
Ethiopia is the best-known center of Arabica diversity.
Research has also confirmed wild Arabica populations in South Sudan's Boma Plateau.
Wild Arabica is not native to South America.

items.termEn: Brazil is the world's top coffee grower and one of its biggest coffee-drinking nations.
items.explanationShort:
Brazil produces more coffee than any other country by volume.
Unlike most coffee-growing nations, it is also one of the biggest consumers, drinking much of what it grows.
Brazil sets the scale for world coffee.

items.termEn: Robusta coffee from Indonesia ends up in many espresso blends and instant coffees.
items.explanationShort:
Indonesia grows large quantities of robusta, which thrives at lower altitudes and in heat.
Because it is available and lower-cost, Indonesian robusta is often used in commercial blends and instant coffees.
Indonesian robusta, often blended.

items.termEn: Coffee grows in roughly the same climate zone as cocoa and bananas.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee plants need consistent warmth, humidity, and no frost to thrive.
That combination only exists in the band between the two tropics.
Coffee needs warmth, humidity, and no frost.

items.termEn: Most of the world's coffee is produced in tropical countries.
items.explanationShort:
The four largest producers, Brazil, Vietnam, Colombia, and Ethiopia, all sit in or near the tropics.
Together they supply roughly two thirds of the world's coffee.
Temperate countries drink it, tropical countries grow it.

items.termEn: Fairtrade mainly certifies roast quality and flavor precision.
items.explanationShort:
Fairtrade focuses on the trading relationship between buyers and farmers.
Its goal is to guarantee fairer prices and more stability for small producers.
Fairtrade is about trading terms for producers, not cup scoring.

items.termEn: A certification logo on a coffee bag does not necessarily mean it was grown organically.
items.explanationShort:
Certification logos cover different standards, such as trading conditions, environmental practices, or organic production.
Only a recognized organic certification establishes that the product meets that organic standard.
A sustainability logo by itself does not automatically mean organic.

items.termEn: High-altitude coffees often taste brighter and more layered than low-altitude ones.
items.explanationShort:
At high altitude, cooler temperatures slow the growth of the coffee cherry.
That slower development gives the bean more time to build density and a more complex flavor.
Grow it higher, taste it deeper.

items.termEn: Coffee prices can rise even if people do not drink more coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee prices respond to supply, not just demand.
A smaller harvest reduces available supply, and that alone is enough to push prices up.
Bad harvest, higher price, same demand.

items.termEn: Coffee can grow well in any climate if enough water is used.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee needs a specific combination of altitude, temperature, and rainfall to develop properly.
Extra water cannot compensate for the wrong climate or soil conditions.
Climate decides where coffee grows, not water.

items.termEn: A mocha at a coffee shop is espresso with chocolate syrup and milk.
items.explanationShort:
A mocha is built like a latte, with espresso and steamed milk, plus chocolate syrup.
The name comes from the Yemeni port of Mocha, once the world's main coffee trading hub.
Mocha is a drink with chocolate, not a special coffee bean.

items.termEn: The Ethiopian coffee ceremony can last more than an hour.
items.explanationShort:
The ceremony includes roasting, grinding, brewing, serving, conversation, and repeated rounds of coffee.
Its pace is deliberately social rather than rushed.
A full ceremony can extend well beyond a quick coffee break.

items.termEn: Coffee professionals use shared references such as the Coffee Taster's Flavor Wheel to describe aromas and flavors.
items.explanationShort:
The SCA Flavor Wheel and the World Coffee Research sensory lexicon give tasters a shared vocabulary.
A roaster's tasting notes are still an interpretation of a specific coffee.
Shared language helps make those descriptions more consistent.

items.termEn: Coffeehouses first became popular in Europe before spreading to the Arab world.
items.explanationShort:
Coffeehouses first appeared in Yemen and spread through the Ottoman Empire in the 15th century.
They only reached Europe two centuries later, in the 17th century.
Arab world first, Europe after.

items.termEn: Turkish coffee culture is recognized on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
items.explanationShort:
Turkish coffee was formally inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
The recognition covers not just the brewing method but also the hospitality rituals and social role it plays.
UNESCO listed it as living heritage, still practiced today.

items.termEn: The clearest early evidence of coffee drinking points to Yemen.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee plants are native to Ethiopia, but the earliest clear drinking culture points to Yemen.
Yemeni Sufi communities used coffee to stay awake during night prayers.
Plant from Ethiopia, drink culture from Yemen.

items.termEn: Turkish coffee is served as a clear, filtered drink.
items.explanationShort:
Turkish coffee is simmered slowly in a small metal pot, then poured directly into the cup.
Because it is unfiltered, the grounds settle at the bottom of the cup.
Turkish coffee arrives with grounds, not as a clear filtered cup.

items.termEn: Mocha was originally the name of a Yemeni port before it became the name of a chocolate coffee drink.
items.explanationShort:
Mocha was first the name of a port city in Yemen, long associated with the coffee trade.
Only later did the word mocha become the name of a chocolate coffee drink.
Place name first, drink name later.

items.termEn: Indian coffee is rarely exported outside Asia.
items.explanationShort:
India grows both arabica and robusta in its southern states of Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu.
That coffee is then exported to Europe and other international markets.
Indian coffee travels farther than most people think.

items.termEn: A long black is made by pouring espresso over water, not water over espresso.
items.explanationShort:
A long black typically starts with hot water in the cup, followed by espresso.
An americano is commonly built by adding water to espresso, although café recipes vary.
Same core ingredients, different conventional order.

items.termEn: A mocha tastes richer and sweeter than a latte because of the chocolate.
items.explanationShort:
A latte is just espresso and steamed milk, with nothing extra added.
A mocha uses the same base but adds chocolate syrup, making it sweeter and richer.
Same base, chocolate changes everything.

items.termEn: Nitro cold brew is cold brew coffee infused with nitrogen gas.
items.explanationShort:
Nitro cold brew is made by infusing cold brew with nitrogen gas under pressure.
The nitrogen creates tiny bubbles that give the drink a creamy, velvety texture without any milk or sugar.
Cold brew plus nitrogen, not cold brew plus milk.

items.termEn: Nitro cold brew always contains added sugar or cream.
items.explanationShort:
Nitrogen creates the creamy texture and cascading appearance of nitro cold brew.
Sugar and cream are optional additions, not requirements of the drink.
Nitro does not mean sweetened.

items.termEn: An extra espresso shot adds roughly 20 mg of caffeine to any drink.
items.explanationShort:
Espresso-shot caffeine varies with coffee, dose, and recipe, but one shot normally adds far more than 20 mg.
The exact number is not fixed from café to café.
An extra shot adds the caffeine contained in that shot.

items.termEn: Adding vanilla syrup automatically increases a coffee drink's caffeine.
items.explanationShort:
Standard vanilla syrup adds sweetness and flavor, not espresso or brewed coffee.
The drink's caffeine still comes mainly from its coffee base.
Some specialty flavorings can contain caffeine, so the ingredient matters.

items.termEn: Coffee often tastes better after a short rest from the roast date.
items.explanationShort:
Right after roasting, beans release CO2 for a few days.
After that short rest, flavor often becomes more balanced before freshness fades.
Fresh does not always mean same-day fresh.

items.termEn: Ordering half-caf at a coffee shop cuts the caffeine by roughly half.
items.explanationShort:
Half-caf is a blend of equal parts regular and decaf coffee.
The result has roughly half the caffeine of a regular cup.
Half the name, half the caffeine.

items.termEn: Adding milk to an espresso reduces its caffeine content.
items.explanationShort:
Milk changes volume, texture, and flavor, but it does not remove caffeine from the espresso already in the cup.
A latte made with a given espresso dose retains that dose's caffeine.
Milk dilutes concentration, not total caffeine.

items.termEn: Using blends does not mean a roaster is compromising on quality.
items.explanationShort:
Blends can be designed deliberately for balance, consistency, body, or a particular espresso profile.
High-quality coffee can be sold as either a blend or a single-origin lot.
Blend is a format, not a quality verdict.

items.termEn: Extra hot on a latte means the milk is steamed beyond the standard temperature.
items.explanationShort:
Standard steamed milk is warm and comfortable to hold through the cup.
Extra hot pushes it past that point, closer to scalding.
Hotter milk, same drink.

items.termEn: A manual espresso machine generally gives the user more brewing control than a capsule machine.
items.explanationShort:
Manual espresso setups can let the user change variables such as grind, dose, yield, and sometimes temperature or pressure.
Capsule systems automate or fix many of those choices.
Manual usually means more control, not automatically better coffee.

items.termEn: A larger latte always contains more caffeine than a smaller one.
items.explanationShort:
The caffeine in a latte comes entirely from the espresso shots, not from the cup size.
A large and a small latte made with the same number of shots carry exactly the same caffeine.
In a latte, cup size adds milk first, not automatic caffeine.

items.termEn: A pour-over and a drip machine both work by passing hot water through ground coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Both a pour-over and a drip machine work on the same principle: hot water flowing through grounds in a filter.
The difference is that a pour-over is controlled by hand, while a drip machine automates the process.
Same principle, different level of control.

items.termEn: A strong coffee does not necessarily taste bitter.
items.explanationShort:
Strength refers to how much dissolved coffee is in the water, not to bitterness.
A well-made strong coffee can taste bold and rich with no harshness at all.
Strong is quantity, bitter is a flavor.

items.termEn: Almond milk can separate in hot coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Plant milks can become unstable when they meet heat and coffee acidity.
Almond milk is one example that may separate depending on the product and preparation.
Barista formulations are designed to improve stability.

items.termEn: The United States is the world's biggest coffee-consuming country per person.
items.explanationShort:
The US is one of the world's largest coffee markets by total volume.
But per person, Nordic countries like Finland consume far more.
Big market, not the biggest per cup.

items.termEn: Coffee consumption in China has grown rapidly in recent years.
items.explanationShort:
China still has a strong tea culture, but coffee consumption has risen quickly, especially in large cities.
Younger urban consumers have helped drive that growth.
Tea still leads, but coffee is rising fast.

items.termEn: Buying a coffee with a Fairtrade label guarantees it was grown organically.
items.explanationShort:
Fairtrade certification focuses on trading conditions like minimum prices and fair contracts, not farming methods.
A Fairtrade coffee can still be grown with conventional pesticides unless it also carries an organic label.
Fair price is not the same as organic farming.

items.termEn: Viennese coffeehouse culture was added to Austria's national intangible cultural heritage inventory in 2011.
items.explanationShort:
The Austrian Commission for UNESCO lists Viennese coffeehouse culture in Austria's national inventory of intangible cultural heritage.
The entry dates to 2011.
It is a national inventory entry, not the UNESCO Representative List of Humanity.

items.termEn: The mineral content of brewing water can change how coffee extracts and tastes.
items.explanationShort:
Minerals and alkalinity affect extraction and perceived acidity.
Water that is very hard or very low in minerals can produce different results.
Water chemistry is part of the brewing recipe.

items.termEn: Mexico produces coffee, but far less than countries like Brazil, Vietnam, or Colombia.
items.explanationShort:
Mexico is a real coffee producer, especially in states like Chiapas and Oaxaca.
But its output is much lower than the biggest producing countries.
Mexico grows coffee, just not at world-leading scale.

items.termEn: Coffee processing after harvest leaves the flavor basically unchanged.
items.explanationShort:
After harvesting, the coffee cherry can be removed and dried in different ways: natural, washed, or honey.
Each method leaves a distinct flavor imprint on the bean before it even reaches the roaster.
Processing shapes flavor long before roasting.

items.termEn: Espresso means pressed out in Italian, not fast coffee.
items.explanationShort:
The word espresso comes from the Italian verb esprimere, meaning to press out.
It describes the act of forcing pressurized water through the grounds, not the speed of preparation.
Pressed, not rushed.

items.termEn: Daily coffee drinkers can build tolerance to caffeine over time.
items.explanationShort:
With regular use, the body can become less sensitive to caffeine.
That means the same cup may feel weaker than it once did.
Same dose, smaller effect.

items.termEn: Coffee dehydrates you enough to cancel out the water in the drink.
items.explanationShort:
Caffeine has a mild diuretic effect, but the water in coffee outweighs it.
That is why moderate coffee consumption still counts toward daily fluid intake.
The water in coffee still counts.

items.termEn: The SCA's current definition of specialty coffee is broader than an 80-point score.
items.explanationShort:
The SCA now defines specialty coffee through distinctive attributes and significant extra value in the marketplace.
An 80-point score is an important historical convention, but it is not the whole current definition.
Specialty is broader than one number.

items.termEn: Coffee accounts for virtually all caffeine in a typical American diet.
items.explanationShort:
Caffeine also appears in tea, chocolate, soft drinks, and certain medications.
Coffee may be the dominant source for most adults, but it is far from the only one.
Coffee leads, but others follow.

items.termEn: Cold foam is just regular steamed milk foam served cold.
items.explanationShort:
Cold foam is made by aerating cold milk or a cold milk-based mixture without steaming it.
That creates a foam designed for cold drinks.
The defining difference is that the foam is made cold.

items.termEn: Coffee and alcohol are safe to mix because caffeine cancels out alcohol's effects.
items.explanationShort:
Caffeine masks the feeling of intoxication but does not reduce the alcohol in the body.
Because people feel more alert, they often underestimate how much they have drunk.
Caffeine hides the effect, not the alcohol.

items.termEn: A lungo uses more water through the coffee puck than a regular espresso.
items.explanationShort:
Lungo means "long" in Italian.
The shot is allowed to run longer, so more water passes through the same coffee dose than in a standard espresso recipe.
More water through the puck is the defining idea.

items.termEn: A ristretto uses less water and a shorter extraction than a regular espresso.
items.explanationShort:
Ristretto means "restricted" in Italian.
It uses a shorter yield from the same general espresso method, producing a smaller, more concentrated drink.
Less beverage is collected than for a regular espresso.

items.termEn: Traditional espresso recipes often target a shot time around 20 to 30 seconds.
items.explanationShort:
Around 20 to 30 seconds is a common traditional reference window for espresso.
Modern recipes can intentionally run faster or slower depending on dose, grind, yield, and coffee.
It is a reference, not a universal law.

items.termEn: Running an espresso longer than its target time automatically makes it smoother.
items.explanationShort:
Shot time is one diagnostic variable, not a guarantee of taste.
If a shot runs much longer than the intended recipe, grind or flow may be off and extraction can become unbalanced.
Longer does not automatically mean smoother.

items.termEn: Drip coffee has one universal ideal brew time of exactly 4 to 6 minutes.
items.explanationShort:
Brew time depends on brewer design, batch size, grind, flow rate, and recipe.
Four to six minutes is a common reference for some drip brewers, not a universal rule for every setup.
Method decides the useful time window.

items.termEn: A bad coffee harvest in Brazil can push up coffee prices far beyond Brazil.
items.explanationShort:
Brazil is the world's largest coffee producer, so a weaker harvest can tighten global supply.
When supply drops, prices can rise well beyond the producing country itself.
Bad harvest in Brazil, higher prices far away.

items.termEn: Single origin coffee can come from one farm, one region, or one country.
items.explanationShort:
Single origin means the coffee comes from one geographic origin, not from a blend of multiple origins.
That origin can be as specific as a farm or as broad as a country.
One origin, different levels of precision.

items.termEn: Coffee spread smoothly everywhere it went and won instant approval.
items.explanationShort:
In the 16th century, coffee was banned in several cities including Mecca and Cairo.
Authorities feared that coffeehouses were becoming centers of political debate and social unrest.
Popular enough to be banned, too popular to stay banned.

items.termEn: Coffee reached Europe through Arab world and Ottoman Empire trade routes.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee traveled from Yemen into the Ottoman Empire and then westward through Mediterranean trade routes.
Venice was one of the first European cities to receive it, in the late 16th century.
Arab world to Ottoman Empire to Europe.

items.termEn: Turkish coffee belongs almost exclusively to Turkey.
items.explanationShort:
Turkish coffee is finely ground coffee simmered in a small pot and served unfiltered, grounds and all.
The method is used across the Middle East, the Balkans, and many other countries.
Same method, many countries.

items.termEn: A bad harvest in Brazil or Vietnam can push up prices at local coffee shops.
items.explanationShort:
Brazil and Vietnam together supply roughly half of the world's coffee.
When either country has a bad harvest, global supply drops and prices climb as a result.
Farm problems abroad, higher prices at home.

items.termEn: Ottoman Empire coffeehouses were social spaces where people gathered to talk, share news, and debate.
items.explanationShort:
Ottoman coffeehouses brought together people from all walks of life under one roof.
They gathered there to discuss politics, listen to music, and exchange news and ideas.
The coffeehouse was the social media of its time.

items.termEn: A skinny latte delivers a lighter caffeine hit than a regular latte.
items.explanationShort:
Skinny refers to the type of milk used, low-fat or non-fat.
Because the number of shots stays the same, the caffeine content is identical to a regular latte.
Less fat, same caffeine.

items.termEn: Sufi Muslims in 15th-century Yemen drank coffee to stay awake during night prayers.
items.explanationShort:
Sufi communities in 15th-century Yemen used coffee to stay alert during long night prayers.
Pilgrims visiting Mecca encountered the practice there and carried it back to Cairo, Damascus, and Istanbul.
Yemen to Mecca to the world.

items.termEn: The paper coffee filter was invented before the modern espresso machine.
items.explanationShort:
Melitta Bentz invented and patented the paper coffee filter in Germany in 1908.
Achille Gaggia's modern espresso machine, which produced crema, did not appear until the 1940s.
Filter first, crema decades later.

items.termEn: Most coffee farms are huge estates larger than 100 acres.
items.explanationShort:
A large share of the world's coffee producers are smallholders working relatively small plots.
Large estates exist, but they do not represent the typical coffee farmer everywhere.
Coffee production includes millions of small farms.

items.termEn: Sufi communities in Yemen were among the first to drink coffee.
items.explanationShort:
The earliest records of coffee as a beverage point to Sufi communities in Yemen.
They valued it for keeping worshippers awake and focused during long nighttime prayers.
Coffee started as a spiritual aid, not a morning ritual.

items.termEn: The term specialty coffee was first used by Erna Knutsen in 1974.
items.explanationShort:
Erna Knutsen first used the term in a 1974 trade article.
She used it to describe high-quality beans with traceable origins, laying the foundation for the specialty coffee movement.
One woman, one term, one industry shift.

items.termEn: Peet's Coffee was founded before Starbucks.
items.explanationShort:
Alfred Peet opened his first shop in Berkeley in 1966, focused on quality beans and fresh roasting.
His philosophy directly inspired the founders of Starbucks, who came five years later.
Peet came first, Starbucks followed.

items.termEn: Starbucks originally sold roasted beans and brewing equipment, not espresso drinks.
items.explanationShort:
When Starbucks opened in Seattle in 1971, it was a bean and equipment store, not a cafe.
Espresso drinks only became central later, after Howard Schultz brought back the Italian coffee bar model.
Beans first, lattes later.

items.termEn: Howard Schultz did not found Starbucks, but he turned it into a global chain.
items.explanationShort:
Starbucks was founded in 1971 by three partners in Seattle.
Howard Schultz joined later, bought the company in 1987, and led its worldwide expansion.
Not the founder, but the builder.

items.termEn: Starbucks was still a small Seattle-area company before Howard Schultz expanded it.
items.explanationShort:
Starbucks began as a small coffee retailer in Seattle.
Howard Schultz later turned it into a much larger coffeehouse chain.
Small retailer first, global chain later.

items.termEn: Erna Knutsen built her own coffee importing business after working in a male-dominated coffee trade.
items.explanationShort:
Knutsen entered a coffee business in which women had limited access to professional roles such as cupping.
She later founded Knutsen Coffees and became an influential figure in specialty coffee.
Her career helped open doors in the trade.

items.termEn: American coffee shops copied Italian espresso bars almost exactly.
items.explanationShort:
American coffee shops borrowed ideas from Italian espresso bars, but changed the format significantly.
Drinks became larger, seating became more central, and the experience was built for people to stay longer.
Italian inspiration, American format.

items.termEn: The first Starbucks store sold espresso drinks from day one.
items.explanationShort:
The original Starbucks, opened in 1971, sold roasted beans and brewing equipment.
It was only after Schultz's 1983 trip to Italy that the espresso bar model was introduced.
Beans first, lattes came later.

items.termEn: Third wave coffee culture focuses on craft, origin, and flavor quality.
items.explanationShort:
Third wave coffee treats coffee more like wine, with attention to origin, processing, and preparation.
The focus shifts from convenience to craft and flavor.
Craft first, convenience second.

items.termEn: Erna Knutsen, who coined the term specialty coffee, was born in Norway.
items.explanationShort:
Knutsen was born in Norway in 1921 and emigrated to the United States.
She coined the term specialty coffee and became one of the most influential figures in the industry.
Norwegian roots, American coffee revolution.

items.termEn: Howard Schultz was the original founder of Starbucks.
items.explanationShort:
Starbucks was founded in Seattle in 1971 by three partners: Baldwin, Siegl, and Bowker.
Howard Schultz only entered the picture in 1987 when he bought the company, 16 years later.
He built it, but did not start it.

items.termEn: An espresso tonic is made by mixing espresso with tonic water.
items.explanationShort:
An espresso tonic combines espresso with chilled tonic water, usually over ice.
The result is fizzy, bitter-sweet, and coffee-forward.
The drink contains no alcohol unless something else is added.

items.termEn: A German woman named Melitta Bentz invented the paper coffee filter in 1908.
items.explanationShort:
In 1908, Melitta Bentz punched holes in a tin pot and used blotting paper from her son's notebook as a filter.
She patented the invention and founded the Melitta company, which still sells filters today.
One woman, one idea, cleaner coffee forever.

items.termEn: The Melitta brand is named after its founder.
items.explanationShort:
When Melitta Bentz founded her company in 1908, she named it after herself.
Over a century later, the Melitta brand is still selling paper filters worldwide.
Her name outlasted her by a century.

items.termEn: The term third wave coffee was coined by a woman named Trish Rothgeb.
items.explanationShort:
Trish Rothgeb introduced the term in a 2003 article while reflecting on coffee culture in Norway.
She used it to describe a movement that approached coffee the way wine lovers approach wine, with attention to origin and craft.
Third wave, coined by a woman.

items.termEn: The International Coffee Organization tracks global coffee production and trade data.
items.explanationShort:
The ICO is an intergovernmental body that collects and publishes data on coffee production, exports, and prices.
Governments, roasters, and traders rely on its data to understand the global market.
The global coffee numbers start with the ICO.

items.termEn: Fairtrade International certifies coffee brands for flavor quality.
items.explanationShort:
Fairtrade certification sets standards for trading conditions and minimum prices paid to farmers.
It says nothing about flavor, aroma, or how the coffee will taste in the cup.
Fair trade is about terms, not taste.

items.termEn: Smallholder family farms play a major role in global coffee production.
items.explanationShort:
Millions of coffee producers are smallholders who cultivate coffee on relatively small farms.
Large estates also contribute to global supply.
Small farms are a central part of the coffee economy.

items.termEn: Melitta Bentz first tested her paper filter using blotting paper from her son's notebook.
items.explanationShort:
In 1908, Melitta Bentz punched holes in a tin pot and lined it with blotting paper from her son's school notebook.
That simple experiment led to the modern paper coffee filter.
School paper, global invention.

items.termEn: One of the earliest patents for an espresso-machine precursor was filed in Italy in 1884.
items.explanationShort:
Angelo Moriondo patented a steam-based coffee machine in Turin in 1884.
Later inventors such as Bezzera and Gaggia developed machines closer to modern espresso.
Espresso-machine history is a sequence of Italian innovations.

items.termEn: Achille Gaggia invented the very first espresso machine.
items.explanationShort:
The first espresso machine patent dates to 1884, decades before Gaggia entered the picture.
What Gaggia contributed in the 1940s was the high-pressure piston that produces the crema we associate with espresso today.
He made espresso modern, not first.

items.termEn: Bean freshness, grind, dose, and machine pressure can all affect espresso crema.
items.explanationShort:
Crema depends on gases in roasted coffee and on the way espresso is extracted.
Freshness matters, but so do recipe and machine variables.
A weak crema has more than one possible cause.

items.termEn: The word barista is originally English.
items.explanationShort:
Barista comes from the Italian word for a person who works behind a bar.
As espresso culture spread from Italy to the rest of the world, the word came with it.
Italian word, global job.

items.termEn: The SCA Flavor Wheel was updated in 2016 with World Coffee Research.
items.explanationShort:
The original Flavor Wheel was published in 1995.
In 2016, the SCA revised it using the World Coffee Research sensory lexicon to create a more structured shared vocabulary.
The update made professional flavor descriptions more consistent.

items.termEn: Espresso culture originated in France.
items.explanationShort:
The espresso machine was invented and first patented in Italy in 1884.
France has a rich café culture, but the espresso machine and method both came from Italy.
Italy invented it, the world adopted it.

items.termEn: The Ethiopian coffee ceremony is considered a symbol of hospitality and community.
items.explanationShort:
The Ethiopian coffee ceremony is a social ritual built around hospitality, conversation, and community.
UNESCO has supported Ethiopia in preparing a nomination for possible future inscription on the Representative List.
Its cultural importance does not depend on already being inscribed.

items.termEn: Soldiers helped make instant coffee a mass-market habit during the world wars.
items.explanationShort:
Instant coffee became useful because it was light, fast, and easy to prepare.
Military use helped normalize it for large numbers of people.
War made instant coffee practical, then familiar.

items.termEn: A moka pot produces espresso.
items.explanationShort:
A moka pot uses steam pressure to push hot water through ground coffee, but at much lower pressure than an espresso machine.
It makes a concentrated coffee, but it is a different brewing method from espresso.
Moka coffee is not technically espresso.

items.termEn: The word coffee is thought to derive from the Arabic word qahwa.
items.explanationShort:
The Arabic word qahwa traveled through Turkish as kahve before entering European languages.
Both the English word coffee and the French café trace back to that same Arabic root.
Arabic root, global word.

items.termEn: The Coffee Taster's Flavor Wheel was first published by the SCA in 2016.
items.explanationShort:
The Flavor Wheel was first published in 1995, then updated in 2016 with World Coffee Research.
The 2016 version made the tasting vocabulary more precise.
First published in 1995, updated in 2016.

items.termEn: Decaffeinated coffee has been commercially available for over a century.
items.explanationShort:
The first commercial decaffeinated coffee was developed in Germany around 1903.
By the 1920s and 1930s, it was already widely available, well before World War II.
Decaf predates most people's grandparents.

items.termEn: Many coffees from Guatemala are arabica grown at high elevations.
items.explanationShort:
Guatemala is known for arabica production in mountainous growing regions.
Higher elevations can shape how coffee cherries mature and how the cup tastes.
Origin can suggest growing conditions, but it does not guarantee quality.

items.termEn: Shifts in temperature and rainfall leave coffee production largely unchanged.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee depends on stable temperature and rainfall patterns to grow well.
When those conditions shift, yields and quality can both suffer.
Climate changes the cup long before it changes the map.

items.termEn: Kona coffee from Hawaii is often sold at a premium compared with many coffees grown elsewhere.
items.explanationShort:
Hawaii has high land and labor costs, and Kona is a limited, well-known origin.
Those factors can push retail prices well above many other coffees.
Premium pricing is common, but exact rankings change with the market.

items.termEn: Costa Rica produces mainly robusta coffee.
items.explanationShort:
Costa Rica is best known for arabica production.
The country historically restricted robusta planting, but those restrictions were relaxed, so "arabica only by law" is no longer accurate.
Robusta is not the country's main coffee.

items.termEn: Global coffee consumption is higher today than it was in the 1990s.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee consumption has grown steadily over the past few decades.
Much of that growth has come from expanding coffee markets outside the traditional coffee-drinking countries.
More countries, more coffee, more cups.

items.termEn: Buying organic coffee guarantees farmers were paid a fair price for their beans.
items.explanationShort:
Organic certification concerns a defined set of farming and processing standards.
It does not by itself guarantee what price the farmer received.
Organic and fair-trade claims answer different questions.

items.termEn: Morning coffee prices are shaped by the same global markets that trade oil and gold.
items.explanationShort:
Coffee is traded on global commodity markets, just like other major raw materials.
A drought in Brazil or frost in Colombia can move coffee prices far beyond the farm.
Global prices shape what ends up in the cup.

items.termEn: A large drip coffee can contain as much or more total caffeine than one or two espresso shots.
items.explanationShort:
Espresso is more concentrated per ounce, but drip servings are much larger.
Total caffeine depends on coffee species, dose, extraction, and serving size.
Concentration and total caffeine are not the same thing.

items.termEn: Cold brew concentrate can contain more caffeine per ounce than drip coffee before dilution.
items.explanationShort:
Cold brew concentrate uses a high coffee-to-water ratio, so it can contain more caffeine per ounce before dilution.
Long steeping is part of the method, but caffeine extraction can level off well before 12 to 24 hours.
The recipe ratio matters more than steep time alone.

items.termEn: A coffee bag's roast date tells you more about freshness than the expiration date.
items.explanationShort:
Date labels on shelf-stable foods generally describe quality, not the moment a product becomes unsafe.
A roast date tells you when the coffee was roasted, which is more useful for judging freshness.
For freshness, roast date matters most.

items.termEn: Milk residue left on a steam wand for a few hours can affect the next drink.
items.explanationShort:
Milk residue dries quickly on the steam wand and can contaminate the next drink.
It affects both cleanliness and flavor if it is not wiped off right away.
Leftover milk can affect the next drink.

items.termEn: Ordering an extra shot on a two-shot drink adds 50 percent more caffeine.
items.explanationShort:
If a drink starts with two espresso shots, adding one more shot takes it from two to three.
That means the espresso caffeine increases by 50 percent, not 100 percent.
Extra shot means more caffeine, not necessarily twice as much.

items.termEn: Specialty coffee can cost more because distinctive lots and coffee experiences can carry extra market value.
items.explanationShort:
The SCA's current definition links specialty coffee to distinctive attributes and significant extra value in the marketplace.
Quality, scarcity, traceability, processing, and other attributes can all contribute to price.
A higher price is not itself proof of specialty.

items.termEn: Ready-to-drink coffee has become a major category in the US coffee market.
items.explanationShort:
Canned and bottled coffee now occupy a growing share of shelf space in US stores.
The category has expanded well beyond a niche convenience product.
Coffee now competes on the grab-and-go shelf too.

items.termEn: Ordering a latte extra hot adds more espresso to the drink.
items.explanationShort:
"Extra hot" changes the target milk temperature, not the espresso dose.
Unless the customer also orders another shot, the espresso quantity stays the same.
Hotter milk does not mean more espresso.
